key_insight: Large language models can internally resist externally applied activation steering during inference — a phenomenon called Endogenous Steering Resistance (ESR). Llama-3.3-70B shows substantial ESR while smaller Llama-3 and Gemma-2 family models exhibit it less frequently.
problem_solved: Addresses the surprising unreliability of activation-steering interventions: models can recover mid-generation toward task-aligned outputs even while steering remains active, undermining assumptions about steerability and intervention effectiveness.
method: Apply sparse autoencoder (SAE) latent vectors to steer model activations during inference and observe behavioral effects.
Compare model responses across families and sizes (e.g., Llama-3.3-70B vs smaller Llama-3 and Gemma-2 variants) to quantify ESR prevalence.
Identify and analyze SAE latents that correlate with resistance and locate where in the model internal recovery emerges.
impact: Practitioners should not assume activation steering will always control model behavior; ESR implies steering can be transiently bypassed, so robustness, evaluation protocols, and steering strategies must account for model-size-dependent endogenous resistance.
visual_elements: Timeline diagram showing steering applied during generation and the model's mid-generation recovery (before, during, after steering).
Bar chart comparing ESR occurrence rates across model sizes/families (e.g., Llama-3.3-70B vs smaller models).
Schematic of SAE latent injection into transformer activations (input → SAE latents → activation modulation → output).
Activation heatmap highlighting SAE latents correlated with resistance and their layerwise influence.
paper_title: Endogenous Resistance to Activation Steering in Language Models
paper_authors: Alex McKenzie, Keenan Pepper, Stijn Servaes, Martin Leitgab, Murat Cubuktepe
